items.prompt: A DynamoDB table receives most requests for a small range of partition-key values. What design change should be evaluated first?

options.text: Choose a partition-key design that distributes requests and storage across partitions, using a composite or write-sharded key when the access pattern requires it.
Increase read capacity without changing a permanently hot key.
Add a sort key and assume it distributes requests across physical partitions.
Put every item in one partition to simplify queries.

feedback.Reason: DynamoDB request distribution is driven primarily by partition-key values, so a concentrated key can create a hot partition.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB partitions data and traffic using partition-key values; a hot key concentrates load even when table capacity is higher.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect models key frequency and introduces a bounded sharding or composite-key strategy while preserving queryability.
Details.errorCorrection: More capacity does not repair a pathological key, a sort key does not change the partition-key routing, and one partition is a bottleneck.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Sharding improves distribution but requires fan-out reads or deterministic aggregation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Extra table capacity cannot make one hot partition distribute itself.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The partition key, not the sort key, determines the initial partition placement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A single partition cannot sustain distributed high traffic.

items.prompt: A single tenant generates a burst of writes to one logical key, but the application can query several deterministic suffixes. Which pattern fits?
constraints: The application can fan out reads.
Write ordering is not required across shards.

options.text: Add a deterministic write-shard suffix to the partition key and fan out or aggregate reads across the bounded shard set.
Use a random sort key while retaining one hot partition key and make no read changes.
Disable throttling so the hot key can consume unlimited capacity.
Move all writes to a single global secondary index partition.

feedback.Reason: Write sharding spreads a hot logical workload across multiple partition-key values when the read path can reconcile shards.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Distinct partition-key values can be placed and served independently; a deterministic suffix lets the writer distribute load.
Details.scenarioApplication: The service writes tenant#0 through tenant#N and queries the known shard set with bounded parallelism.
Details.errorCorrection: A sort key does not distribute a single partition key, throttling cannot be disabled, and a single index key can be hot too.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Fan-out increases read cost and application complexity and must be bounded.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A random sort key still routes all items under the same partition key.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Throttling is a protection signal, not a control to remove capacity limits.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: An index with one concentrated key merely moves the hot spot.

items.prompt: A new workload has highly unpredictable traffic and no reliable forecast for capacity planning. Which capacity mode should be evaluated?
constraints: The team accepts per-request pricing analysis.

options.text: Evaluate DynamoDB on-demand capacity, comparing its automatic request handling and per-request cost with the workload's steady-state and burst profile.
Provision the peak observed rate forever without measuring utilization.
Use provisioned mode with zero capacity because DynamoDB will queue all requests durably.
Use a cache as the durable source for writes.

feedback.Reason: On-demand mode is designed for workloads where capacity needs are difficult to predict and request-based pricing is acceptable.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB on-demand capacity serves requests without customer-managed read and write capacity units, subject to service limits and behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner observes request volume, latency, throttles, and cost before deciding whether a stable workload merits provisioned capacity.
Details.errorCorrection: Peak provisioning can overpay, zero provisioned capacity does not queue unlimited work, and caches are not durable write stores.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: On-demand pricing can be higher for sustained predictable volume and must still respect key distribution and quotas.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Capacity should be based on measured demand rather than one peak forever.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Requests are not an unlimited durable queue when capacity is absent.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A cache is not the durable system of record.

items.prompt: A DynamoDB workload is predictable on weekdays but grows and shrinks by season. What control should be compared with on-demand mode?
constraints: The owner wants utilization-based capacity changes.

options.text: Evaluate provisioned capacity with Application Auto Scaling, target utilization, minimum and maximum capacity, and a scale-out lead time based on the workload.
Set capacity to the monthly average and ignore bursts and scaling delay.
Set maximum capacity to zero during quiet periods and assume existing requests remain available.
Add a global secondary index without sizing its write capacity.

feedback.Reason: Provisioned capacity can be economical for predictable traffic when an explicit scaling policy covers variation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Application Auto Scaling adjusts provisioned read and write capacity from CloudWatch metrics within configured bounds.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect chooses targets and bounds from load tests and schedules or pre-scales for known peaks.
Details.errorCorrection: Averages can throttle peaks, zero capacity is not a safe live state, and an index has its own write-capacity requirements.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Provisioned mode can reduce sustained cost but scaling is not instantaneous and consumes capacity planning effort.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Average capacity can be below burst demand and cause throttling.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Capacity cannot be treated as a free durable queue during a live request path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A GSI consumes capacity and needs independent modeling.

items.prompt: A table has mostly balanced keys but occasionally one key receives a short spike. What DynamoDB behavior should be considered before redesigning every key?
constraints: The service behavior is still monitored.

options.text: Consider adaptive capacity as a helpful redistribution behavior, while still validating key distribution, partition limits, and sustained hot-key behavior.
Assume adaptive capacity makes any single key unlimited.
Remove all partition-key diversity because adaptive capacity replaces key design.
Disable metrics because throttles are impossible with adaptive capacity.

feedback.Reason: Adaptive capacity can help uneven access but is not a substitute for a sound partition-key design or service limits.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB can allocate available capacity more effectively to partitions with higher demand under supported conditions.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner verifies consumed capacity, throttles, key frequency, and sustained behavior rather than relying on an assumed unlimited exception.
Details.errorCorrection: Adaptive capacity does not remove all per-partition or item limits and does not justify one key for all traffic.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: It reduces some operational pressure but cannot fix pathological access patterns or unlimited demand.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Adaptive capacity is bounded by service and partition behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Good key diversity remains necessary for durable scale.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Metrics are required to verify whether the workload is actually healthy.

items.prompt: A GSI is added to a provisioned table and writes begin throttling even though the base table has spare write units. What is the likely design issue?
constraints: The index is populated by writes.
Base and index metrics are available.

options.text: Size and monitor the GSI's write capacity and key distribution independently, because indexed writes consume index capacity as well as base-table work.
Increase only base-table write capacity because a GSI has no capacity requirement.
Delete the partition key from the GSI so every item shares one index partition.
Read from the GSI to repair a write-capacity shortage.

feedback.Reason: A provisioned GSI has its own read and write capacity and can become the throttling component.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB propagates relevant base-table writes into a GSI, and the index has separate capacity and partition distribution.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect measures indexed write volume, chooses an even index key, and provisions or autos-scales the GSI.
Details.errorCorrection: Base-table spare units do not guarantee index spare units, a single index key is hot, and reads do not create write capacity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Indexes improve query access but add write cost, storage, propagation work, and another scaling surface.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A provisioned GSI has independent capacity settings.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: One concentrated index key creates a hot index partition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Reading an index cannot increase its write capacity.

items.prompt: A query needs only a few attributes from a GSI and must avoid fetching the base item for every result. Which choice should be made?
constraints: Index storage and write cost matter.

options.text: Project the attributes required by the query into the GSI, choosing the smallest useful projection and measuring index storage and write cost.
Project every attribute into every index regardless of access needs.
Project no attributes and assume the index can return the full item without a fetch.
Store the complete item in a sort key string to avoid projection decisions.

feedback.Reason: A suitable GSI projection can make a query covered while limiting duplicated data and write work.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Projected attributes are stored with index keys; an index query can avoid a table fetch when it contains the needed fields.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner projects only query and response attributes, then measures index size, write amplification, and read latency.
Details.errorCorrection: Projecting everything increases cost, no projection requires a base fetch, and packing items into keys harms the data model.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A wider projection reduces fetches but increases storage and write consumption.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A broad projection duplicates unnecessary data and increases cost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: An index without needed attributes cannot return them without reading the base table.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Keys are not a safe substitute for modeled attributes and projections.

items.prompt: A table needs queries grouped by a partition key and sorted by time, and all items for one group must remain together. Which index constraint matters?
constraints: The query needs alternate sort behavior.

options.text: Evaluate an LSI only if its same-partition-key model and item-collection size constraint fit the growth profile; otherwise model a GSI.
Choose an LSI because it can always use a different partition key from the base table.
Assume an LSI has no item-collection limit because it shares table storage.
Use an LSI to distribute one hot partition across unlimited physical partitions.

feedback.Reason: LSIs share the base table partition key and have item-collection constraints, so they fit only bounded same-key access patterns.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A local secondary index uses the table partition key with an alternate sort key and is limited by the item collection for that key.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect estimates per-key item size and growth before selecting an LSI or moving the access pattern to a GSI.
Details.errorCorrection: An LSI cannot use an independent partition key, is not unlimited, and does not distribute a hot base key.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: LSIs support strongly consistent reads and same-key access but impose modeling and creation-time constraints.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An LSI shares the base table partition key by definition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The item collection size constraint still applies.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: An LSI does not remove a hot base partition key.

items.prompt: An application needs all orders for one customer in a date range and must avoid scanning unrelated customers. Which access pattern should be modeled?

options.text: Use Query with the customer partition key and a sort-key condition for the time range, then paginate results as needed.
Use Scan with a filter for customer and date because filters reduce the read work first.
Use a key condition on a non-key attribute without an index.
Read every item and filter in the client to avoid DynamoDB request limits.

feedback.Reason: A Query uses the key schema to target one partition and a sort-key range instead of reading unrelated items.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB Query requires a partition-key equality condition and can apply a sort-key condition before returning pages.
Details.scenarioApplication: The model stores customer as the partition key and order time as the sort key, with pagination and projection tuned to the response.
Details.errorCorrection: Scan reads the table before filtering, non-key attributes require an index, and client-side full reads waste capacity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A very large customer partition still needs item-size, page, and hot-key analysis.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A filter does not prevent Scan from reading the scanned items.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A key condition applies to key attributes of the table or selected index.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Client filtering transfers and reads data unnecessarily.

items.prompt: A read path can tolerate a small replication delay and prioritizes lower read capacity consumption. Which consistency should be evaluated?
constraints: The item is not immediately read after a write.

options.text: Use eventually consistent reads for eligible requests, documenting the staleness boundary and reserving strong consistency for paths that require it.
Use strongly consistent reads for every request because they are always cheaper.
Use a filter expression to turn an eventually consistent read into a strong read.
Disable replication so all reads are inherently current.

feedback.Reason: Eventually consistent reads can reduce read capacity use when the application accepts propagation delay.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB eventually consistent reads may return a recent prior value, while strong reads request the latest value where supported.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect assigns consistency by use case and tests post-write visibility for user-facing and transactional paths.
Details.errorCorrection: Strong reads are not always cheaper, filters do not change consistency, and replication is part of the service model.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Lower cost and latency can come with bounded staleness; strong consistency can reduce availability or double read-unit consumption.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Strong reads consume more capacity and are not required for every path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Filtering selects returned items but does not change read consistency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Removing a service capability is not a consistency design.

items.prompt: A workflow reads an item immediately after a conditional write and must show the committed state. What should be selected?
constraints: The read occurs after a write.
The table or index supports the required consistency.

options.text: Use a strongly consistent read where supported, and verify that the selected index and global replication path meet the consistency requirement.
Use an eventually consistent read and retry forever without a consistency budget.
Use a Scan because Scan is always strongly consistent by default.
Read from a cache that has not been invalidated by the write.

feedback.Reason: A current-after-write requirement must be mapped to a supported strong-read path rather than assumed from the API name.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Strongly consistent reads return the most up-to-date value for supported table or local-index operations, with documented exceptions.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner chooses the read mode explicitly and uses invalidation or version checks for any cache involved.
Details.errorCorrection: Unbounded retries hide a design issue, Scan is not a universal default for strong reads, and a stale cache can violate the workflow.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Strong reads consume more capacity and can have availability or topology constraints.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Retries do not define a bounded current-read guarantee.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Scan does not make every access path strongly consistent by default.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: An uninvalidate cache can return the pre-write value.

items.prompt: A checkout operation must update several items atomically and reject the whole change if one condition fails. Which DynamoDB capability fits?
constraints: Conditions are part of the business rule.
The operation fits service transaction limits.

options.text: Use a transactional write with explicit condition checks, then size the additional capacity and latency cost and handle retry idempotency.
Issue independent writes and assume network ordering makes them atomic.
Use BatchWriteItem because batch writes always provide all-or-nothing semantics.
Write to a cache first and persist the items later without a recovery plan.

feedback.Reason: DynamoDB transactions provide coordinated all-or-nothing behavior for supported multi-item operations.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: TransactWriteItems applies multiple actions atomically and supports condition checks, with transaction limits and capacity implications.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect uses deterministic client tokens where appropriate and models retries, conflicts, latency, and consumed capacity.
Details.errorCorrection: Independent writes can partially commit, BatchWriteItem is not transactional, and a cache-first path can lose durable state.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Transactions simplify correctness but add coordination cost and limits compared with independent writes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Network ordering does not provide atomic commit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: BatchWriteItem does not provide all-or-nothing transaction semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A cache cannot be the only durable commit path.

items.prompt: A bulk import returns unprocessed DynamoDB write items during a traffic peak. What should the writer do?
constraints: The import can use bounded backoff.

options.text: Retry only the unprocessed items with exponential backoff and jitter, while monitoring capacity, hot keys, and total import rate.
Retry the entire batch immediately in a tight loop.
Discard unprocessed items because the batch API guarantees their persistence.
Increase client concurrency without limit until all requests succeed.

feedback.Reason: Batch APIs can return unprocessed items that the application must handle without amplifying throttling.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: BatchWriteItem reports unprocessed operations so the client can retry them; exponential backoff reduces repeated pressure.
Details.scenarioApplication: The importer persists its input, retries only the remainder with a cap, and records items that exceed the retry policy.
Details.errorCorrection: Immediate whole-batch retries amplify load, unprocessed items are not guaranteed persisted, and unlimited concurrency worsens throttling.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Backoff improves recovery but extends import time and requires idempotent or deduplicated writes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Whole-batch tight retries repeat successful work and amplify load.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Unprocessed items still require application handling.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Unbounded concurrency can increase throttling and cost.

items.prompt: Two workers may create the same order and the operation must not overwrite an existing record. What should be used?
constraints: The client can handle a conditional failure.

options.text: Use a conditional Put or transaction condition such as attribute_not_exists for the key, and treat ConditionalCheckFailedException as a business result.
Use an unconditional Put and let last-writer-wins resolve the race.
Use a Scan before every write and assume the check is atomic.
Write the item to a cache and conditionally persist it later.

feedback.Reason: A conditional write makes the uniqueness rule part of the database operation rather than a separate race-prone read.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB condition expressions are evaluated with the write and can reject a conflicting item atomically.
Details.scenarioApplication: The service treats one successful creator as canonical and returns a safe duplicate response to the loser.
Details.errorCorrection: Unconditional writes overwrite, a Scan-then-write has a race, and a cache is not the authority for uniqueness.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Conditional checks add an evaluation and failure path but protect correctness under concurrency.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Last-writer-wins can silently overwrite a valid order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A separate Scan and write are not one atomic operation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Cache state cannot enforce durable uniqueness safely.

items.prompt: A DynamoDB table reports throttled requests while total table capacity appears sufficient. Which investigation is most useful?
constraints: Per-partition behavior is not yet known.
The key distribution can be sampled.

options.text: Correlate throttled operation, partition-key frequency, consumed capacity, index metrics, account or table quotas, and request bursts before choosing a remediation.
Increase every client timeout and assume the table is undersized.
Delete indexes without checking whether their capacity is the constrained path.
Add retries with no backoff so capacity is used faster.

feedback.Reason: Throttling can come from a hot partition, index, burst, or service quota even when aggregate table capacity looks adequate.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB exposes consumed and throttled metrics at table and index scope, while partition-key concentration can limit effective capacity.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operator identifies the constrained dimension, then changes key design, capacity, traffic shaping, or quota with evidence.
Details.errorCorrection: Timeouts do not add capacity, deleting an index may break access paths, and immediate retries amplify contention.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Diagnosis takes observability work but avoids an expensive and ineffective blanket scale-up.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Timeout changes do not explain or remove the constrained resource.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: An index may be required and must be measured before removal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Retries need backoff and jitter to avoid an amplification loop.

items.prompt: A read returns large items and the team is surprised that one request consumes several read capacity units. What should be explained?

options.text: Capacity consumption depends on item size and consistency, so reduce payload with projection or redesign only when the measured access pattern justifies it.
Assume every item costs exactly one read capacity unit regardless of size.
Use a filter expression because filters make the underlying read free.
Store unlimited attributes in one item because item size has no capacity effect.

feedback.Reason: DynamoDB capacity is calculated from the amount of data read and the selected consistency, not merely request count.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Read capacity consumption is based on item size rounded to service units; strong reads consume more than eventual reads for the same data.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect projects only needed attributes, paginates responses, and separates hot summary data from large documents where useful.
Details.errorCorrection: Size matters, filters do not make reads free, and an item has size and capacity limits.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Projection lowers transferred data but may require another access path or index design.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Read capacity is rounded from item size and consistency mode.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A filter does not erase the read work used to evaluate items.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Large items increase capacity, latency, and item-limit risk.

items.prompt: A multi-Region application needs local reads and writes with conflict handling. What must be part of the DynamoDB design?
constraints: Conflict behavior is a business decision.

options.text: Evaluate a global table with Region-local access, replication lag, conflict resolution, capacity in each Region, and an explicit multi-writer data ownership rule.
Assume global tables provide synchronous cross-Region transactions for every write.
Use a single-Region table and route all writes over the public internet without latency analysis.
Ignore concurrent updates because replicated records always merge semantically.

feedback.Reason: Global tables improve regional access but introduce replication, capacity, and conflict semantics that must be designed.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB global tables replicate table data across Regions and support regional endpoints with documented replication and conflict behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner chooses single- or multi-Region writes, assigns ownership or reconciliation rules, and tests failover and replicated capacity.
Details.errorCorrection: Cross-Region replication is not universal synchronous transaction coordination, internet routing adds latency, and records do not always merge safely.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Regional write locality improves resilience and latency but increases cost and conflict complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Replication and transaction semantics are not equivalent to synchronous global commit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A single Region may violate latency or resilience goals and public routing is not a design shortcut.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Concurrent updates need an explicit conflict policy.

items.prompt: A session table must remove expired records without an application delete job, but expiration is not an exact-time business event. What should be selected?
constraints: Expired data is no longer needed.
Exact deletion time is not required.
The application must not treat expiration as immediate deletion.

options.text: Evaluate DynamoDB TTL for the expiration attribute and design consumers so expired items are treated as unavailable before background deletion completes.
Use TTL as an exact-time trigger for a payment settlement workflow.
Set TTL on the partition key so DynamoDB can choose the expiration time.
Assume TTL deletion immediately frees every related index and stream record synchronously.

feedback.Reason: TTL is useful for eventual removal of expired items, not for an exact-time business transition.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB TTL marks items with an epoch expiration attribute and removes them asynchronously after expiration eligibility.
Details.scenarioApplication: The service rejects expired sessions by timestamp and uses TTL for cleanup rather than relying on deletion timing.
Details.errorCorrection: TTL is not an exact scheduler, requires an expiration attribute, and downstream effects are not an immediate synchronous contract.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: TTL reduces cleanup work but leaves an interval where an expired item may still exist and should be filtered by application logic.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Exact settlement timing requires a workflow or scheduler with explicit guarantees.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: TTL uses an expiration attribute rather than the partition key.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: TTL removal and downstream propagation are asynchronous behaviors.

items.prompt: A table has stable high traffic, a well-understood key distribution, and cost pressure from on-demand requests. What decision should be reviewed?
constraints: The team will monitor utilization and throttles.

options.text: Compare provisioned capacity with auto scaling against on-demand cost using measured read and write demand, peak behavior, key distribution, and operational overhead.
Switch modes solely because provisioned capacity has a lower unit price, without checking peak behavior.
Keep on-demand forever because capacity mode cannot be changed after table creation.
Choose provisioned capacity and remove all alarms because throttling is impossible.

feedback.Reason: Capacity mode is an operational and economic decision that must include demand variability and scaling controls.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB supports capacity-mode choices with different management and billing behavior; provisioned mode requires capacity planning or auto scaling.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner models the full request distribution, pre-scales known peaks, and retains alarms after changing mode.
Details.errorCorrection: Unit price alone ignores bursts, capacity mode can be changed under documented conditions, and provisioned capacity can still throttle.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Provisioned mode can lower steady-state cost but shifts forecasting and scaling responsibility to the owner.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Peak and scaling behavior are required in addition to unit price.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Capacity modes are not immutable in the way described.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Provisioned capacity still needs monitoring and can throttle.
